Officers Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański engaged him, were seriously wounded, but neutralized the attacker, who later died in hospital.

Europe’s security today depends on its unity. European states must jointly define their goals, agree on common action and defend their shared position in negotiations. Otherwise, Moscow and Washington will set the terms on which Europeans will have to live and defend themselves.

The current talks have made particularly clear what Putin is seeking: control over Europe’s security decisions by dividing Europe and weakening its alliances. He is reviving his demands on NATO and rejecting the deployment of European troops in Ukraine as a safeguard against another invasion. Meanwhile, Russian diplomats are proposing non-aggression pacts with individual NATO members. Other proposed models include agreements not to assist the other party’s adversaries.

These proposals point to a way of dividing Europe: replacing collective defence with separate deals between Moscow and individual capitals. Each state could be offered its own “guarantees” in exchange for restrictions on its actions. This would give Russia leverage over individual countries’ decisions and the ability to block a collective response.

Europe’s debate over a common representative matters precisely in this context. The EU already has representatives and a position based on European Council decisions. EU institutions, national governments and partners outside the Union need to coordinate their actions. Meloni is calling for clarity on who speaks for Europe and what they are authorised to negotiate. She does not oppose Costa, but raises the question of how the United Kingdom and Norway would be represented.

Merz supports the E3 — France, Germany and the United Kingdom — and a broader group including Italy and Poland. Macron proposes first agreeing on a concrete plan that would determine the negotiating format. This approach rests on states’ ability to implement agreements. A common mandate must also give other allies, particularly those on the eastern flank, a say in decisions affecting their security.

Costa, Kallas and Stubb have been mentioned as possible representatives. Costa represents EU leaders and has the backing of Luxembourg’s prime minister; Kallas already oversees the Union’s foreign policy; Stubb has direct contacts with Trump and his envoys. Any representative needs clear authority and the support of the governments on whose behalf they would speak.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal believes the necessary representatives are already in place — Costa and Kallas. His main warning concerns the substance of the talks. In exchange for a seat at the table, Europe is being pushed to discuss its own defence with a state that threatens it. This turns Europeans’ right to organise their own defence into a bargaining chip, and restrictions on their security into a possible price paid to Russia for ending its aggression.

Kallas proposes a sensible sequence: a ceasefire, a peace settlement, then discussions on broader European security. Agreements already exist — from the Helsinki Final Act to the Charter of Paris and the Budapest Memorandum. Russia has violated them. Costa also reaffirms Ukraine’s freedom to choose its alliances, the inviolability of borders and the rejection of spheres of influence.

Europe already has the foundation for a unified negotiating position. The joint statement of 10 November and the Dublin Declaration of 12 November set out its main principles: decisions on Ukraine must be made with Ukraine, and decisions on European security with Europeans. States choose their own alliances, NATO remains the foundation of collective defence for its members, and Ukraine must receive credible security guarantees. Discussions on additional risk-reduction mechanisms are envisaged once the necessary conditions have been met and peace has been restored.

These principles must now be translated into a shared strategy and concrete action. Europeans need to agree on their own plan to deter Russia, sustain long-term support for Ukraine, develop joint defence capabilities and coordinate the use of sanctions and financial instruments.

This will enable Europe to set the negotiating agenda and influence the outcome. This is how its agency should be expressed — through its own goals, initiative and capacity to act.

On this basis, a clear negotiating mandate must be agreed: the desired outcome, the limits of possible concessions, ways to verify compliance and the consequences of breaches. The common representative must have the backing of European governments, sufficient resources and those governments’ willingness to implement and uphold agreed decisions together.
